$comment: Published areas of responsibility: the prose, quoted, that the drawn overlay is built from.
The geometry itself lives in src/data/aor-boundaries.ts, generated by
tools/build_aor_boundaries.py from the same statements recorded here. This file is the
reading room: the full published wording for every area, including the ones that are not
Every `statement` is a verbatim quotation. Where the live .mil page refuses automated
requests, the citation is the Internet Archive capture of that official page and both URLs
are given, because the capture is evidence of what the official page said and when.
Schema: schema, revised, boundaryOverlay, combatantCommands[], numberedFleets[].

combatantCommands.name: United States Africa Command
combatantCommands.statement: responsible for operations, exercises, and security cooperation on the African continent, its island nations, and surrounding waters. The area of responsibility consists of 53 African states, more than 800 ethnic groups, over 1,000 languages, vast natural resources, a land mass of 11.2 million square miles (three-and-a-half times the size of the U.S.), and nearly 19,000 miles of coastland.
combatantCommands.drawabilityNote: Drawn from the command's OWN published map data at https://www.africom.mil/data/africajson.js, which declares its base layer as Natural Earth 1:50m admin-0 countries. Western Sahara appears in neither the country list nor the file, so that edge is genuinely unpublished. Egypt is excluded by AFRICOM's own footnote: it sits in U.S. Central Command's area.

combatantCommands.name: United States Indo-Pacific Command
combatantCommands.statement: The USINDOPACOM AOR covers more of the globe of any of the other geographic combatant commands and shares borders with all of the other five geographic combatant commands. ... The 38 nations comprising the Asia-Pacific region are home to 60% of the world's population.
combatantCommands.drawabilityNote: NOT DRAWN, and this is a correction. A previous revision of this file drew USINDOPACOM from the widely-repeated sentence 'from the waters off the west coast of the U.S. to the western border of India, and from Antarctica to the North Pole'. That phrasing could not be sourced to any primary command page in any capture, so the overlay built on it has been withdrawn. What the command actually publishes is a count of nations and a statement that its area borders all five other geographic commands - neither of which is drawable.

combatantCommands.name: United States Northern Command
combatantCommands.statement: USNORTHCOM's AOR includes air, land and sea approaches and encompasses the continental United States, Alaska, Canada, Mexico and the surrounding water out to approximately 500 nautical miles. It also includes the Gulf of Mexico, the Straits of Florida, portions of the Caribbean region to include The Bahamas, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
combatantCommands.drawabilityNote: The only quantitative maritime figure published by any command - and it says 'approximately'.

combatantCommands.name: United States Southern Command
combatantCommands.statement: SOUTHCOM is responsible for providing contingency planning, operations, and security cooperation in its assigned Area of Responsibility which includes: Central America / South America / The Caribbean (except U.S. commonwealths, territories, and possessions)
combatantCommands.drawabilityNote: Named regions with an exception clause. No maritime limit.

combatantCommands.name: United States Central Command
combatantCommands.statement: The new command's area of responsibility (AOR) was designated as the 'central' region of the globe, situated between the European and Indo-Pacific Commands. Over the past four decades, the AOR has evolved to keep pace with a changing world, and as of 2026, it encompasses 21 nations.
combatantCommands.drawabilityNote: A count of nations, positioned relative to two neighbouring commands.

combatantCommands.name: United States European Command
combatantCommands.statement: The USEUCOM area of responsibility covers 50 countries and territories, including Europe, Russia, and parts of Asia and the Middle East.
combatantCommands.drawabilityNote: Drawn from the command's OWN published map data at https://www.eucom.mil/data/europejson.js, minus Israel. The two are not in conflict: the map file carries the GEOGRAPHY, which has not moved, while the command's live country-list page carries the ASSIGNMENTS, and Israel's assignment moved to U.S. Central Command on 15 January 2021. A stable geometry file alongside a current assignment list is exactly what you would expect of a boundary set whose lines hold for years while the states inside them occasionally change hands. This overlay takes the geometry from the file and the assignment from the list. The file also carries five European dependencies - Aland, the Faroe Islands, Guernsey, the Isle of Man and Jersey - which the 50-country prose list does not enumerate.

numberedFleets.name: U.S. 7th Fleet
numberedFleets.statement: Seventh Fleet's area of operations spans more than 124-million square kilometers, stretching from the International Date Line to the India/Pakistan border; and from the Kuril Islands in the North to the Antarctic in the South. Seventh Fleet's area of operations encompasses 36 maritime countries and 50% of the world's population
numberedFleets.drawabilityNote: Drawn, and the only fleet with a published coordinate. The 2013 fact sheet gave the western limit numerically - 'from the International Date Line to the 68th meridian east, which runs down from the India-Pakistan border' - which is the only numeric boundary the U.S. Navy has ever published for any fleet. North and south remain landmarks rather than lines and are drawn open.

numberedFleets.name: U.S. 5th Fleet / U.S. Naval Forces Central Command
numberedFleets.statement: ...encompasses about 2.5 million square miles of water area and includes the Arabian Gulf, Red Sea, Gulf of Oman and parts of the Indian Ocean. This expanse, comprised of 21 countries, includes three critical choke points at the Strait of Hormuz, the Suez Canal and the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb at the southern tip of Yemen.
numberedFleets.sourceName: U.S. Naval Forces Central Command / U.S. 5th Fleet
numberedFleets.drawabilityNote: Drawn. The named seas and the three named choke points fix three sides; 'parts of the Indian Ocean' fixes none, so the seaward edge is indefinite. A previous revision of this file quoted a widely-repeated but unpublished wording ('North Arabian Sea, Gulf of Aden'); that string appears in no capture of the command's own site and has been replaced.

numberedFleets.name: U.S. Naval Forces Europe-Africa / U.S. 6th Fleet
numberedFleets.statement: The Commander, U.S. Naval Forces Europe-Africa (NAVEUR-NAVAF) area of responsibility (AOR) covers approximately half of the Atlantic Ocean, from the Arctic Ocean to the coast of Antarctica, as well as the Adriatic, Baltic, Barents, Black, Caspian, Mediterranean, and North Seas.
numberedFleets.sourceName: U.S. Naval Forces Europe-Africa / U.S. 6th Fleet
numberedFleets.drawabilityNote: Drawn, with the attribution corrected: the Navy publishes this as NAVEUR-NAVAF's area of responsibility, not as 6th Fleet's, and the page title carries both names. 'Approximately half of the Atlantic Ocean' names no meridian, so the western edge is indefinite.

numberedFleets.name: U.S. 4th Fleet / U.S. Naval Forces Southern Command
numberedFleets.statement: USNAVSO/FOURTHFLT employs maritime forces in cooperative maritime security operations in order to maintain access, enhance interoperability, and build enduring partnerships that foster regional security in the USSOUTHCOM Area of Responsibility.
numberedFleets.sourceName: U.S. Naval Forces Southern Command / U.S. 4th Fleet
numberedFleets.drawabilityNote: Defined by reference to USSOUTHCOM's area, which is itself only a list of regions.

numberedFleets.name: U.S. 3rd Fleet
numberedFleets.statement: Operational commands that report directly to the U.S. Pacific Fleet include Third Fleet in the Eastern Pacific and Seventh Fleet in the Western Pacific and Indian Ocean.
numberedFleets.drawabilityNote: Not drawn, and the reason is that the boundary was removed rather than never stated. The 2002 page gave 'approximately fifty million square miles of the eastern and northern Pacific'; the 2015 page gave 'from the West Coast of North America to the international date line'; from 2017 the Date Line clause is gone and the current page gives no area at all. There is no published Date Line exception - the Navy stopped stating the boundary rather than carving one out.

numberedFleets.name: U.S. 2nd Fleet
numberedFleets.statement: Maneuver arm for NAVNORTH, in the Atlantic and Arctic, ensuring freedom of the sea lines of communication. Maneuver arm for NAVEUR in the Eastern and Northern Atlantic. Defend maritime avenues of approach between North America and Europe.
numberedFleets.drawabilityNote: Not drawn. Second Fleet has never published a bounded area in any era, and its current mission page describes it as a manoeuvre arm operating inside NAVEUR's eastern and northern Atlantic - so it does not own an area to draw.

numberedFleets.name: U.S. Fleet Cyber Command / U.S. 10th Fleet
numberedFleets.statement: No geographic area of operations is published for U.S. 10th Fleet. Its published mission is cyber and space, not a maritime area.
numberedFleets.sourceName: U.S. Fleet Cyber Command / U.S. 10th Fleet
numberedFleets.drawabilityNote: Listed here only so its absence from the map is an answer rather than an omission.

boundaryOverlay.headline: Areas of responsibility are drawn from the published wording, with every edge marked as published or indefinite.
howItIsBuilt: Two commands publish their AOR geometry themselves, on their own hosts, and where they do this overlay uses theirs rather than assembling its own. AFRICOM's file declares its base layer as 'ne_50m_admin_0_countries' - the command built its map from public-domain Natural Earth outlines by selecting the assigned states, which is exactly the construction used here. That settles the method question: this is not a workaround for missing data, it is the same method the publisher used.

Combatant-command areas are published as assignments of states, and the familiar Unified Command Plan map is a country-shaded map rather than a survey of lines. Where a command publishes a country list, the overlay colours exactly those countries, using public-domain Natural Earth outlines for the geometry. The authorship of the boundary stays with the command that published the list.

Numbered fleet areas are maritime and are published as prose. Where that prose names a real line - the International Date Line, the India/Pakistan border, the Arctic Ocean, the coast of Antarctica - the overlay draws it. Where it names a landmark or says 'approximately', that edge is marked indefinite and drawn open and faded rather than as a confident line.
The overlay is vendored offline in src/data/aor-boundaries.ts, the same way the coastline artifact is. Nothing is fetched from a third party at runtime, and nothing is traced from a picture.

U.S. Indo-Pacific Command is deliberately NOT drawn, and that is a correction rather than a gap. An earlier version of this overlay drew it from the widely-repeated sentence 'from the waters off the west coast of the U.S. to the western border of India, and from Antarctica to the North Pole'. That phrasing could not be sourced to any primary command page in any archived capture, so the overlay built on it was withdrawn. What the command actually publishes is a count of nations and a statement that its area borders all five other geographic commands, neither of which is drawable.
boundaryOverlay.whatIsNotDrawn: U.S. 2nd, 3rd and 4th Fleet, and U.S. 10th Fleet. Third Fleet's own mission page carries no area text at all; Fourth Fleet is published only by reference to U.S. Southern Command's area; Second Fleet is published as a manoeuvre arm rather than as an area owner; Tenth Fleet has no geographic area by design. Their published wording is quoted below so the absence is an answer rather than an omission.
boundaryOverlay.publicationCadence: The annual vehicle is the Defense Planning Guidance: where a combatant command's geographic boundaries change, that is the document promulgating it. It is not a public document, which is why no annual published boundary map exists - the absence is a classification fact about the vehicle, not evidence that the public record has drifted. The Unified Command Plan itself is classified under 10 U.S.C. 161(b)(1) and is reviewed every two years and as needed.
boundaryOverlay.stability: Two different things change on different timescales, and conflating them is the easy mistake. GEOGRAPHIC BOUNDARIES - the lines themselves - have been stable for many years. COUNTRY ASSIGNMENTS within them move occasionally, and every change this project was able to verify in the public record is of that second kind: Israel from U.S. European Command to U.S. Central Command, announced 15 January 2021, and Greenland from U.S. European Command to U.S. Northern Command, announced 17 June 2025. Neither redrew a line; both reassigned a state. That is why the age of a published map is not the caveat it looks like: a raster from 2011 still depicts the current geography, and its age is evidence that the lines have held rather than evidence that the source has gone stale. What does need watching is the assignment lists, and those the commands keep current on their own pages. This project deliberately puts no date on the last geographic change, because no public source was found that states one.
